source.title: Jacobian Sparse Autoencoders: Sparsify Computations, Not Just Activations
source.authors: Lucy Farnik; Tim Lawson; Conor J. Houghton; Laurence Aitchison

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether SAE dictionaries yield interpretable features in pretrained LLMs, a different measurement relevant to V4. It does not test the original toy-model superposition setup or feature-overlap geometry.
record.gate_note: Only V4 is tested, and only its SAE-feature-recovery aspect: the paper compares SAE latent interpretability and gives interpreted feature examples. It does not test whether features are spread across neurons. The paper’s Jacobian-sparsity, reconstruction, language-model-performance, and linearity findings concern computation between SAE latents, not the superposition versions. Background statements about overcomplete dictionaries are not new results.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It uses SAEs as a tool to propose Jacobian SAEs and reports that method's own performance (Jacobian sparsity, reconstruction, auto-interp parity with standard SAEs, linearity of the latent-to-latent map). It never asks whether LLMs contain sparse features an SAE can recover. Its auto-interp numbers compare two SAE variants and have no non-SAE baseline such as neurons. The latent examples are handpicked illustrations. None of its results bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that JSAEs induce Jacobian sparsity with minimal loss in reconstruction and downstream performance and no degradation in latent interpretability. They add that the discovered computations are often interpretable, that Jacobian sparsity is greater in trained than in random LLMs, and that the MLP in the JSAE basis is mostly linear. They make no claims about superposition itself.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains paired TopK SAEs on MLP inputs and outputs and adds a Jacobian-sparsity loss. It does not reproduce the toy-model feature-overlap method; its focus is computational sparsity in Pythia MLPs.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that Jacobian sparsity and reconstruction/performance measures vary with the Jacobian-loss coefficient, layer, expansion factor, and TopK sparsity. It does not report that these settings change the V4 interpretability comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: Jacobians between input and output SAE latents are much sparser in trained Pythia models than in randomly re-initialized ones, for both traditional SAEs and JSAEs (Fig. 7, Fig. 38).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse computational connectivity between dictionary features is a learned property of trained LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: The MLP rewritten in the SAE basis is mostly linear. Of the scalar latent-to-latent functions, 88% are linear, 10% JumpReLU and 2% other; 97.7% of Jacobian values predict the change from a large intervention.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLP computation between SAE features is approximately linear.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The interpretability comparison is a proxy based on an LLM fuzzing scorer, and exact values are not stated in the text. Qualitative feature examples are selected rather than systematic. The study does not establish ground-truth feature recovery, completeness, or stability, and does not test the broader superposition claim.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on V1–V6 were omitted. Results on Jacobian sparsity, reconstruction quality, model-performance preservation, and approximate linearity were left out because they concern computational mappings between SAE latents rather than the versions tested here.

untested.parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, the sparsity transition and regular geometry: none studied.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure: not studied.
No test of whether features are spread across neurons. No SAE-versus-neuron or trained-versus-random comparison of feature interpretability; the paper only cites Heap et al. for the latter.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features: not studied.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features: not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' reading and its V4 'supports' label are dropped. Parity of auto-interp scores between two SAE variants says nothing about whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features, and the qualitative latents are handpicked illustrations. Background statements about overcomplete dictionaries are cited, not tested.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure or are evidence against superposition.

The study evaluates SAE-feature interpretability in Pythia models, but does not test whether features are distributed across many neurons or establish that the SAE features are a complete account of model representations.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

relation.reason: The reported results concern JSAE performance, computational sparsity and latent-to-latent mappings; feature recovery is used as methodological background rather than independently tested.

tranche.reason: The study uses sparse dictionary representations to develop and evaluate computational sparsity methods. Its SAE comparisons and selected qualitative examples do not independently test the listed superposition claims.

source_check.notes: R1–R4 are method comparisons with figure-only scores; R5–R6 are selected qualitative illustrations. Their cannot_determine states and lack of version links are appropriate; the authors-conclusion paraphrase matches the text.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-410m and Pythia-70m SAE latents evaluated with the fuzzing scorer; selected Pythia-410m examples
reader_labels.reason: JSAE latents have interpretability scores described as similar to traditional SAE latents, and selected latents receive interpretable descriptions; this supports the SAE-feature-recovery aspect of V4, but not its neuron-distribution alternative (R1–R6).
